summary: This unit teaches you to deal with the problems that come up again and again in a villa, hotel, restaurant or attraction: to spot a problem, find the facts and the real cause, decide what you can solve and what you must report, choose a safe solution, act on it, check that it worked, and record it so it does not happen again.

blocks.p: Every workplace has problems: a tap that drips, a guest who is not happy, a delivery that is late, a machine that stops. A **familiar problem** is one of a kind that often comes up in your job. You can learn how to deal with them, and that is what makes you a worker that supervisors trust.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. It does not ask you to fix everything yourself. It asks you to think clearly, stay safe, keep to your role, ask for help at the right time, and follow through.

blocks.h: Dealing with a problem, step by step

flow: Notice it and make it safe
Say clearly what the problem is
Gather the facts
Find the cause

Check that it worked
Record it and share what you learned

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper with multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays, and two group practical tasks. In the first you find about eight problems in the Centre's mock villa, fix those you are allowed to fix, make the others safe, tag faulty items and report them. In the second you study a case file from a hotel, find the root cause of a repeat problem with the '5 whys', and make an action plan. Use made-up names and details.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In the mock villa, never touch the inside of an electrical item or a damaged cable. Put out a wet floor sign before mopping, wear gloves, and lift boxes with your knees bent and your back straight.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Spotting the problem and finding its cause

blocks.h: What a familiar problem looks like

head: Area
Examples of familiar problems
rows: Housekeeping
Vacuum cleaner stops; stained towel; empty soap dispenser; blocked drain; a guest's lamp does not work
Food and beverage
A dish is sold out; the till stops; a glass breaks; the chiller is warm; clean glasses run short
Front office
A room is not ready; a guest loses a key card; a booking is mixed up
Attractions and tours
A bus breaks down; a long queue; a guest feels faint; heavy rain
Team
A co-worker is often late; two people argue about a task; a new worker is not trained

blocks.p: These are different from **emergencies** (a fire, a serious injury) and from **unusual problems** that you have never seen before. Emergencies need immediate action by the emergency procedure. Unusual problems should go to your supervisor.
A small problem, such as a dripping tap, should be dealt with early. Small problems grow, cost more to fix and upset guests.

blocks.h: Step 1: make it safe and say what the problem is

ul: First, check that **people are safe**: guests, co-workers and you. Keep people away from danger before you do anything else.
Then say clearly, in one sentence, what the problem is. 'The water in room 4 is cold' is clear. 'Something is wrong with room 4' is not.
Do not blame anyone yet. Blame does not fix anything.

blocks.p: Ask five questions, and write the answers down.

head: Question
Example: guests say the hot water runs out
rows: What is happening?
The shower runs cold after a few minutes.
Where?
In the three upstairs rooms, not downstairs.
When?
Every morning between 7 and 8 a.m.
Who is affected?
Guests in rooms 5, 6 and 7.
How often and how long?
Each day this week; for about 15 minutes each time.

blocks.p: Getting the facts stops you guessing. It also helps the person who comes to repair the problem.

blocks.h: Step 3: find the cause, not only the signs

blocks.p: The **signs** of a problem are what you see. The **cause** is why it happens. If you deal only with the signs, the problem comes back.

head: Sign
Possible cause
Fixing only the sign
Fixing the cause
rows: Wet floor in the store room
A leaking pipe above
Mop it every day
Report the leak so maintenance fixes the pipe
The walk-in chiller is warm in the afternoon
The door is left open during deliveries, or the seal is damaged
Move the food to another fridge every day
Change the delivery routine, and have the seal repaired
Breakfast starts late
The bread arrives late
Serve breakfast without bread
Ask the baker to deliver earlier

blocks.p: Moving the food to another fridge is right for today, because it protects the food. But it is a short-term fix. The problem is only solved when the cause is found.

The **5 whys** is a way to reach the **root cause**: the main reason a problem happens, which must be fixed to stop it coming back. You ask 'Why?' again and again, until the answer is something you can change. Here is an example.

head: Question
Answer
rows: The pool towels ran out at 11 a.m. Why?
Only 30 towels were put out.
Why only 30?
That is what the checklist says.
Why does the checklist say 30?
It was written when the villa had fewer guests.
Why was it not updated?
Nobody is responsible for updating it.
Why?
Nobody has told the supervisor that the number is too low.

blocks.p: The root cause is that the checklist is out of date and nobody reports shortages. The solution: report the shortage and ask the supervisor to update the checklist. You do not always need exactly five whys: stop when you reach something you can fix.

blocks.note: Keep your 'whys' about **things and routines**, not people. 'Because Sam is lazy' does not help. 'Because nobody told Sam the new routine' does.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Your **authority** is what your job role and the property's rules allow you to do. Acting within your authority keeps you, the guests and the property safe. Ask yourself four questions:

ol: Is it safe for me to deal with?
Is it part of my job role?
Do I have the skills, tools and permission?
Does it cost money, or need a decision about rules, refunds or other staff?

head: Usually you can solve it yourself
Report it to your supervisor
rows: A guest needs extra towels
A bin is full
An empty soap dispenser
A wet floor (put out a sign, dry it)
A stained towel to replace
Boxes blocking a walkway
A spark from a switch, a damaged cable or a smell of burning
A leaking pipe or a blocked drain
A broken lock or an air conditioner that does not work
A guest asks for a refund, a free item or a different room
An injury, a lost child or a theft
Any problem that is unsafe or outside your skills

blocks.note: Never try an electrical, gas or plumbing repair unless it is your job and you are trained. Even a simple-looking job can cause a fire, a shock or a flood.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Report it as soon as you can
Choose a place where guests cannot hear, unless it is urgent
Speak calmly and stick to the facts
Say what, where, when, who is affected, and what you have already done
Say what you think the cause is, if you know
Ask what the supervisor wants you to do next
Write it down

ul: Do not blame people, and do not say how angry you are.
If your supervisor is away, tell the person in charge of the shift.

For a guest's repair request, find out who deals with it: the **maintenance** (engineering) team for repairs, **housekeeping** for cleaning and supplies, **front office** for bookings, keys and room moves, **security** for safety and strangers.

blocks.p: Speaking is quick, but a written record means the problem is not forgotten, the next shift knows, and someone can check it later.

head: Record
What it is for
What to write
rows: Log book
Messages and problems for the next shift
Date, time, your name, the problem, the place, what was done, what is still to do
Maintenance request form
A repair job for the maintenance team
Date, room or place, a clear description, how urgent, who reported it
Incident or accident report
An injury or something serious that happened
Who, what, where, when, what was done, who was told, witnesses

blocks.p: A good record is clear, factual and complete, with a date, time and name. Writing it down also shows you reported it.

sections.title: Choosing and carrying out a solution

blocks.h: Think of more than one option

blocks.p: The first idea is not always the best. List several options, perhaps with your team. **Brainstorming** is a group method of listing as many ideas as possible, quickly, before judging any of them. Do not criticise ideas during the brainstorm.

head: Ask
Why
rows: Is it **safe**?
Rule out anything that could harm a guest or a worker.
Is it **allowed**: within my authority and the rules?
If not, ask for approval.
What does it **cost**, and how long will it take?
Some solutions are too expensive or too slow for the problem.
What **tools, people or stock** are needed?
Do you have them?
What is the effect on **guests**?
Choose the solution that disturbs them least.
Does it fix the **cause**, or only the sign?
A short-term fix may be needed now, but aim to fix the cause.

blocks.p: Example: breakfast is late because the bread arrives at 8 a.m. Options: serve breakfast without bread; send someone to buy bread; start breakfast later; ask the baker to deliver by 6 a.m. The last one fixes the cause, costs little and does not disturb guests, so it is the best. Your supervisor must agree it first.

ul: Agree the solution with your supervisor if it is not clearly within your role. Do not change it into your own idea afterwards.

Follow the property's **procedures**: written steps for common tasks, also called **SOPs** (standard operating procedures). Look first in your department's procedures manual, not on social media or from a friend at another hotel.
Work safely: wear gloves, put out signs, keep guests away.
Keep guests informed, politely: say what is happening and about how long it will take.
Have a **plan B**: a back-up plan if the first plan cannot work. Examples: if rain starts, the wedding moves to the covered terrace; if the till stops, use the paper back-up bills.

head: Situation
Short-term action
Report or fix for good
rows: The till (point-of-sale system) stops at lunch
Use the back-up paper bill pads; add the sales later
Report the fault to the supervisor or IT; record the bills
Rain starts during an outdoor event
Move to the plan B venue; protect the equipment
Review the plan with the manager
A supplier does not deliver on Sunday
Tell the supervisor so stock can be borrowed or bought
Ask for orders to be changed for the weekend

blocks.note: A solution that is not allowed, such as using your own money and charging the guest, or moving stock without permission, can cause bigger problems than the one you were solving.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Safety problems come first. A **hazard** is anything that could cause harm, such as a wet floor, a loose stair rail or a trailing cable. Deal with a hazard before it hurts anyone.

head: Hazard
What to do
rows: Wet floor or a spill
Put out a wet floor sign at once
Clean and dry it; keep guests away until it is dry
Report a leak so the cause is fixed
Oil or grease on a kitchen floor
Put a sign out, cover it with absorbent material, clean it up straight away
Do not walk round it and leave it
Boxes blocking a walkway or a fire exit
Clear them at once and tell the supervisor
Fire exits must be clear at all times
Broken step, loose rail or damaged path
Stop people using it: stand by it, put out signs, cones or tape
Report it to maintenance with the exact place
Do not repair it unless it is your job
Faulty electrical item
Stop using it; label it 'Do not use'; report it
Never wrap tape round a cut cable and carry on
Broken glass
Make the area safe; sweep it up with a brush and pan, not with bare hands; wrap it before putting it in the bin
Chemicals
Use as the label says; check the safety data sheet (SDS) for the facts on a chemical; never mix cleaning chemicals; keep them in labelled containers

blocks.h: A spark or a smell of burning

flow: Keep people away
Do not touch the switch or the wires
Switch off at the main board or by the proper method only if it is safe and you know how
Report it at once to the supervisor and maintenance
Tag it 'Do not use'

ul: Raise the alarm and call the fire brigade on **110** (the emergency number for fire and ambulance in Jamaica; police are on 119).
A **pan of oil on fire**: turn off the heat if it is safe, and cover the pan with a lid or a fire blanket. **Never throw water** on an oil fire, and never carry the burning pan.
Use an extinguisher only if you have been trained and the fire is small, and keep your exit behind you.
Guests and staff leave by the nearest safe exit and go to the assembly point. Never use a lift in a fire.

blocks.h: When someone is hurt or unwell

flow: Check that the area is safe for you and for them
See if they are hurt and what help they need
Call a trained first aider, and the ambulance on 110 if serious
Stay with the person and keep them calm
Tell the supervisor
Fill in an incident report as soon as you can

ul: A **first aider** is a worker trained to give first aid. Know who they are and where the first aid box is.
Do not move a person who may have a back or neck injury unless there is danger.

A **near miss** is an event where nobody was hurt, but somebody easily could have been, for example a guest who nearly slips on a wet step. Report near misses too. They warn you before an injury happens.
An **incident report** is the written report after an accident, injury or serious event. It states the facts only: who, what, where, when, and what was done.
Keep guests away and put out a sign. Wear disposable gloves.
Cover the vomit or blood with absorbent material, scoop it into a bag, clean the area with detergent, then disinfect it, as the procedure says.
Seal the bag, put it in the right bin, remove the gloves, and **wash your hands** well.
Report it, and record it if the property requires.

blocks.h: A missing child or a lost guest

blocks.p: Follow the lost-child procedure and alert staff at once. Get a description, a photo if possible, where and when the child was last seen. Staff block the exits and search while one person stays with the parent. Be kind to the parent: do not ask why they did not watch the child. Call the police if the child is not found quickly.

ul: Jamaica's hurricane season runs from June to November. When a storm warning is given, follow the property's **storm plan**: secure or bring in loose items such as pool furniture and umbrellas, charge torches and phones, check the supplies of water and food, tell the guests what is happening, and listen to official warnings.
Do it early. Do not wait for the storm to arrive and then decide.
Keep fridge and freezer doors closed. Food stays cold longer: a fridge keeps cold for about 4 hours if the door stays shut, and a full freezer longer.
Use battery lamps or torches, not candles, because candles are a fire risk. Take care on stairs and in dark corridors.
A generator should be started and run only by someone trained, **outside** and well ventilated, never in a closed room, because it gives off a poisonous gas.
Tell guests calmly what has happened and how long it is likely to last. Use the back-up paper bills if the till is down.
Afterwards, check the fridge temperature (it should be 5 °C or below). If food has been above that for too long, tell the supervisor, and throw it away if told to.

flow: Stop using it
Switch off and unplug it only if it is safe
Label it 'Do not use'
Report it to the supervisor and maintenance
Fill in a request
Check the repair when it is done

ul: A **Do not use** label stops other people from using the item before it is repaired. Do not put it back in the store for the next shift.
When maintenance repairs something, check it yourself: switch on the repaired air conditioner and see that the room cools, rather than trusting the note.
Never use a faulty item 'just this once', and never pass it on to a guest.
Check your stock before a busy time, such as a weekend or a holiday, and tell the supervisor when it is low. This is preventing a problem.

If the store is empty and the supplier is closed, tell your supervisor so that stock can be found elsewhere. Do not take items from another department without telling anyone, and do not buy with your own money and charge the guest.
Keep a record of what ran out and when, so the order level can be changed.
Check each delivery against the order. Look at quantity, quality, dates and condition.
Chilled food must arrive cold (5 °C or below), frozen food frozen. If a delivery arrives warm or damaged, refuse it or report it, and record the problem.
A repeat late delivery is a sign of a cause to fix: speak to the supervisor so the supplier can be asked to change the time.

flow: Listen without interrupting
Apologise and thank the guest for telling you
Ask questions to understand
Do what is within your role
Pass on what is not, and tell the guest what will happen and roughly when
Follow up to check that the guest is satisfied
Record it

ul: Be calm and polite, even if the guest is not. Do not argue or blame another department.
Offer something you can do straight away, such as a cold drink, a seat or a fan, while the problem is being fixed. Offer a bigger step, such as another room, only with the supervisor's approval.
Never promise something you cannot deliver.

head: Familiar guest problem
A good response
rows: Room not ready at arrival
Greet warmly, offer a drink and somewhere comfortable to wait, give a time, store their bags safely, tell housekeeping to hurry the room.
A guest loses a room key card
Check their identity against the booking before making a new card. Never give a key to someone who just asks.
Air conditioner stops working at night

Check only the simple things you are allowed to check (switch, remote, setting). Call the on-call maintenance or the supervisor. Offer a fan, water or another room if free. Log it for the day team and follow up.
A guest says she has an allergy
Never guess. Check with the chef before she orders, and tell the kitchen. Take it seriously every time.
A guest has had too much to drink and is rude
Stay calm, stop serving them politely, and call a supervisor. Do not argue and do not ask other guests to deal with him.
A guest feels faint at an attraction
Find a shaded place to sit, offer water, call a first aider, and report at once.

ul: Two co-workers arguing about whose turn it is: talk calmly and agree a fair schedule. A **compromise** is an agreement where each side gives up a little to settle a problem.
A co-worker is often late and you keep doing extra: speak to the co-worker politely first. If it continues, speak to your supervisor. Do not copy them, complain online or stop doing your own work.
A new worker does not know how to use a machine safely: show the steps or ask the supervisor to train them. Do not let them learn by trial and error with dangerous equipment.
At a **team meeting** after a busy shift, talk about the problem calmly, without blaming. Gather the facts, find the cause, list options, choose together, and agree who will do what and by when.

blocks.note: Example: servers keep running out of clean glasses at dinner. The team finds that dirty glasses stay on the tables and the glass washer is started late. They agree on a person to clear glasses at busy times, start the glass washer before service, and check the result after a week.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The last step of solving a problem is to **evaluate**: check whether the solution worked. Without a check, the problem may still be there, and the next guest may suffer.

ul: Look at the result yourself: switch on the light, check that the fridge is cold, see that the floor is dry.
Ask the guest or co-worker who was affected whether things are better.
If it has **not** worked, do not hide it. Tell your supervisor, look at the problem again to find what was missed, and try another option or ask for help from someone with more skills.
Record each thing you tried, so that people do not repeat the same failed fix.

blocks.p: A record such as a log book entry makes sure the problem is not forgotten and shows the next shift what happened. Over time, records show **patterns**: for example, the same villa toilet blocks every week, or the freezer alarm goes off every Friday. Then the cause can be found and fixed for good.

head: A good record includes
Why
rows: Date and time
So it can be put in order and followed up
Place
So that people can find the problem
What the problem was
So that others understand it
What was done and by whom
So that nothing is repeated or missed
The result and anything still to do
So that the next shift can finish the job

ul: Check bar stock, linen and supplies before a busy weekend.
Check equipment at the start of the shift: lights, taps, locks, machines, extinguisher in its place.
Fix small problems early, report near misses and listen to what guests say.
Follow the storm plan and other plans in good time.
Share what you learned with the team after a problem is solved. Do not keep it secret in case you are blamed. Finding a problem is not a fault; hiding one is.
I can explain what a familiar problem is and why small problems should be dealt with early.
I can make an area safe, say what the problem is, and gather the facts with what, where, when, who and how.
I can tell the signs of a problem from its cause, and use the 5 whys to reach the root cause.
I can decide whether I can solve a problem myself or must report it, by checking safety, role, skills and cost.
I can report a problem by speaking and in writing, with the facts and what I have done.
I can list options, brainstorm, compare them for safety, cost, time and effect on guests, and choose the best one.
I can follow procedures, and use a plan B.
I can deal with wet floors, spills, blocked exits, faulty equipment and broken glass.
I can describe what to do in a kitchen fire, a spark from a switch, an injury, a missing child, a storm and a power cut.
I can respond to a guest's problem by listening, apologising, acting within my role and following up.
I can help to settle a problem in the team calmly and fairly.
I can check that a solution has worked, and try another if it has not.
I can write a clear log book entry, maintenance request and incident report.
I can help prevent problems and share what I learned.

terms: A problem of a kind that often comes up in your job.
A sudden, serious problem that puts people in danger and needs action at once.
What you can see, such as a wet floor.
Why the problem happens, such as a leaking pipe.
The main reason a problem happens, which must be fixed to stop it coming back.
Asking 'Why?' again and again to reach the root cause.
What your job role and the rules allow you to do.
The book where staff write problems and messages for the next shift.
A form asking maintenance to repair something.
Listing many ideas quickly, before judging any of them.
Standard operating procedure: the written steps for a task.
A back-up plan if the first plan cannot work.
An agreement where each side gives up a little.
A worker trained to give first aid.
An event where nobody was hurt but someone easily could have been.
The written report after an accident, injury or serious event.
Safety data sheet: the safety, storage and first-aid facts for a chemical.

c1.title: A damp patch in room 4, Port Antonio
c1.text: A guest at a small hotel in Port Antonio tells the room attendant, Camille, that room 4 smells musty and that there is a brown damp patch on the ceiling near the ceiling light. After last night's heavy rain, drops of water are falling onto the carpet. The guest is annoyed, and her suitcase is open on the bed below the patch. The hotel has two other rooms free, and Camille's supervisor, Mrs Wright, is at the front desk.

c2.title: Pool towels run out in Treasure Beach
c2.text: At a villa resort in Treasure Beach, the pool opens at 9 a.m. The attendant puts out 30 towels, which is the number on the checklist. By 11 a.m. all towels are gone and guests complain. The 40 guests include families who have come from breakfast. The laundry returns clean towels at 10:30 a.m. The attendant, Delroy, notes that the checklist was written when the villa had fewer guests.

c3.title: A guest feels unwell at breakfast
c3.text: At breakfast in a hotel in Mandeville, a guest, Mr Reid, 70, suddenly says he feels dizzy and sick. He then vomits on the floor beside his table. Other guests are close by. A server, Natalia, is nearest, and the hotel has a trained first aider on duty. The restaurant is busy.

c4.title: A power cut during dinner service
c4.text: At 7:30 p.m. on a Saturday, the electricity supply fails during dinner at a hotel restaurant in Mandeville. The restaurant is full, the kitchen goes dark, the till stops and the walk-in chiller goes quiet. A new worker finds candles in a drawer and wants to light them on every table. The generator is in a closed storeroom behind the kitchen, and the head cook says he will start it there.

c5.title: Late linen and an argument
c5.text: At a hotel in Montego Bay, housekeeping and the laundry staff are arguing. The room attendants say the clean linen arrives at 11 a.m., so rooms are not ready for the 2 p.m. check-in. The laundry staff say that housekeeping brings the dirty linen back after 3 p.m., so the machines start late the next day. Both teams blame each other. Their supervisor, Mr Edwards, asks them to find a solution.

questions.q: What is the 'sign' and what is the likely 'cause' of the problem in room 4?
o: The sign is the damp patch and drips; the cause is probably a leak from the roof or a pipe above
The sign is the damp patch and drips; the cause is the heavy rain, which no one can fix, so nothing can be done
The sign is the musty smell; the cause is the guest's open suitcase lying on the bed under the damp patch
The sign is the guest's complaint; the cause is an old carpet that soaks up water and makes the room smell
questions.why: The sign is what you can see: the patch, the drips and the smell. The cause is why it happens, such as water coming through the roof or a pipe. Fixing only the sign, such as wiping the carpet, leaves the leak.

questions.q: Water is dripping near the ceiling light. What should Camille do first?
o: Keep the light switched off, move the guest and her things out of the room, and report it to Mrs Wright and maintenance
Switch the light on to see how bad the leak is, then wipe the water up with a towel and report it at the end of the shift
Climb on a chair to look at the ceiling light, since she can see better from there what is wrong with it
Place a bucket under the drips, tell the guest it is fine to stay, and ask the guest to avoid the light
questions.why: Water near electrical fittings is a shock and fire risk. Make people safe, keep the light off, and report it. Camille should not inspect or repair the fitting, and should not leave a guest in an unsafe room.

questions.q: Camille needs to move the guest to another room. Whose decision is this, and why?
o: Mrs Wright's, as a room move changes the bookings and needs the supervisor's approval
Camille's, as she is the room attendant who found the problem and the guest is upset about it
The guest's, as she can choose any room she wishes in the hotel without any approval
Maintenance's, as they will decide where the guests sleep when a room is out of use
questions.why: Room moves affect the booking, the rate and the room status, so the front desk or supervisor decides. Camille can explain what is happening, offer help with the bags, and pass the request on.

questions.q: Camille reports the leak to Mrs Wright. Which information should she give?
o: Room 4, ceiling by the light, since last night's rain, dripping, and what she has already done
That room 4 has a problem, and that the guest is very upset and wants to speak to the manager at once
That the maintenance team should have fixed the roof before the rain, as it has leaked before in the rooms
That the guest says the hotel is dirty, and that she thinks the guest will leave a bad online review
questions.why: A good report gives the facts: what, where, when, who is affected and what has been done. Opinions, blame and guesses about reviews do not help the problem to be fixed.

questions.q: What is the best first step for Delroy in finding out why the towels run out?
o: Gather facts: how many guests use the pool, when the towels go, and how long laundry takes
Put out as many towels as he can find, then see if anyone complains the next day
Ask the guests to bring their own towels from their rooms, so that the pool never runs short
Tell the supervisor that the guests take too many towels and need to be told to stop
questions.why: Facts come before solutions. Counting guests, times and the laundry cycle shows the cause. Guessing, or blaming guests, does not.

questions.q: Which answer is closest to the root cause of the problem?
o: The checklist number is out of date and was never changed when guest numbers rose
Guests use the pool for longer on Saturdays, so they use more towels than they need
The laundry returns the towels at 10:30 a.m., so there is no way to get more earlier
Delroy does not count the towels carefully when he puts them out at 9 a.m. each day
questions.why: Asking 'why?' leads back to a routine that can be changed: the checklist was written for fewer guests. The late laundry is a related cause, but the fixed number of 30 is what makes the towels run out.

questions.q: Which solution is the best to suggest to the supervisor?
o: Raise the number put out at 9 a.m. to match guest numbers, and update the checklist
Put out all the towels from the store at 9 a.m., even if some may be needed in the rooms
Tell guests there are only 30 towels and they must return them after 20 minutes
Close the pool until 11 a.m. when the clean towels are back from the laundry
questions.why: This solution is safe, cheap, quick and fixes the cause. The others affect guests, may leave the rooms short, or lose the pool's use during the busiest time.

questions.q: The new number has been used for one week. What should Delroy do next?
o: Check whether the towels still run out, ask guests, and record the result in the log
Stop thinking about it, as the problem was solved when the checklist was changed
Increase the number again each day, without checking, to make sure it will not run out
Report that the supervisor made the wrong decision if the towels run out even once
questions.why: The last step is to evaluate: check that the problem is really fixed, and record it. If it has come back, look at the cause again and try another option.

questions.q: Mr Reid says he is dizzy and sick. What should Natalia do first?
o: Help him to sit safely, stay with him, and call the first aider and her supervisor
Start cleaning up the floor before the other guests notice, then go back to taking orders
Tell him to go back to his room at once and lie down so that he will not disturb others
Give him a glass of water and a strong coffee, then ask him to go outside by himself
questions.why: The person comes before the mess. Keep him safe, do not leave him alone, and get the trained first aider. The supervisor should be told, and an incident report written afterwards.

questions.q: After Mr Reid has been helped away, how should the vomit be cleaned up?
o: Keep guests away, wear gloves, scoop it up, clean, disinfect, bag it and wash her hands
Mop it with the usual mop and bucket and then put a fan on the floor to dry it quickly
Throw some paper napkins on top and ask the cleaner to sweep it up at the end of service
Pour bleach on it and leave it until it dries, then sweep it up with a dry broom
questions.why: Vomit can carry germs. Wear gloves, soak it up, clean, then disinfect, and wash your hands. The area must be kept clear and signed until it is safe.

questions.q: What should be written afterwards about Mr Reid's illness?
o: An incident report with who, what, where, when, and what was done and by whom
A note in the guest book saying that Mr Reid was unwell and left early
Nothing, since he became ill by himself and was not hurt in the restaurant
A message on the hotel's social media page so other guests know what happened
questions.why: Serious events are recorded in an incident report, with the facts only. Guests' health details are private, and must not be shared online or with other guests.

questions.q: Which should be done first when the power fails in the full restaurant?
o: Keep guests calm and safe, tell them what is happening, and use battery lamps or torches
Ask guests to leave, then lock the doors and wait for the electricity to come back on
Keep serving the meals, since guests can eat without any light for the rest of the evening
Ask the guests to use their phone torches for the whole evening, to avoid extra costs
questions.why: People's safety and calm come first. Battery lamps and clear information keep everyone safe. Sending guests away or serving in the dark are not safe or professional.

questions.q: The new worker wants to light candles on every table. What should be said?
o: Use battery lamps instead, because candles are a fire risk, especially in a crowd
Go ahead, because candles will give a pleasant atmosphere while there is no power
Light them only in the kitchen, where there is more space, and keep them away from guests
Light candles on the tables, but ask the guests to move any menus well away from them
questions.why: Candles near people, cloth and paper cause fires, and a power cut makes a fire harder to handle. Battery lamps and torches are safer.

questions.q: The head cook says he will start the generator in the closed storeroom. What is the problem?
o: It gives off a poisonous gas, so it must be run outside in the open air by a trained person
The storeroom is too small, so the generator would get too hot to start properly
The generator needs the kitchen door open so that the noise does not disturb the guests
It is not allowed, because only the electricity company may start a generator on a hotel property
questions.why: Generators produce carbon monoxide, which can kill. They must be run outdoors in a ventilated place and operated only by a trained person.

questions.q: What should staff do about the food in the walk-in chiller during the cut?
o: Keep the door closed, and check the temperature when the power returns
Open the door often to check that the food is still cold at every few minutes
Move all the food to ice boxes right away, even if the cut lasts only a few minutes
Throw out all the food at once, whatever the length of the power cut
questions.why: A closed chiller stays cold for hours. Opening it lets cold air out. Afterwards check the temperature (5 °C or below) and tell the supervisor if food has been too warm for too long.

questions.q: What is the best first step for Mr Edwards?
o: Bring both teams together, calmly, to share the facts about times and what each needs
Decide who is at fault and tell that team to change what they do, with a warning
Ask each team to keep working as they are, since they will sort it out in time
Tell the room attendants to wash the linen themselves in the evening, after their shift
questions.why: Team problems are solved by facts, not blame. Meeting calmly, with both sides, lets the cause be found: here, two timings that depend on each other.

questions.q: Which solution is a good compromise for both teams?
o: Housekeeping returns dirty linen by 1 p.m., and laundry delivers the clean linen by 9 a.m.
Laundry delivers the clean linen at 11 a.m., and housekeeping returns the dirty linen at 3 p.m.
Laundry takes over the room attendants' job of checking the linen in each room each morning
Housekeeping buys extra sets of linen with its own money so it never needs to wait for laundry
questions.why: A compromise means each side changes a little. Earlier return of dirty linen lets laundry start earlier, and earlier delivery lets rooms be ready by 2 p.m. The other options keep the problem or shift costs.

questions.q: The teams try the new times for two weeks. How should they check that the solution works?
o: Record how many rooms are ready by 2 p.m., and ask the front desk and both teams
Ask only the laundry team whether they are happy with it, because they started the argument
Assume that it works because the argument has stopped and everybody is being polite now
Go back to the old times after one day, if even one room is still late for check-in time
questions.why: To evaluate a solution you need facts: rooms ready on time, plus views from the people affected. If the problem remains, look at the cause again and adjust the plan.

questions.q: A guest nearly slips on a wet step by the pool, but does not fall. Nobody is hurt. What should you do?
o: Make the step safe, report it as a near miss, and record it in the log
Do nothing, since nobody was hurt and there is no need to report anything
Tell the guest to be careful next time, and say that pool steps are always wet
Write an accident report and send it to the police, because it could have been serious
questions.why: A near miss is an early warning. Reporting it lets the cause be fixed before someone is hurt. It is not an accident, so it needs a log or near miss report, not a police report.

questions.q: You know a quicker way to clean the coffee machine than the written procedure. What should you do?
o: Follow the procedure, and suggest your idea to your supervisor
Use your quicker way when your supervisor is out, to save time on busy days
Teach the quicker way to the new staff, so that everyone can finish sooner
Follow the procedure only when a guest or manager is watching what you are doing
questions.why: Procedures keep work safe and consistent. If you think there is a better way, suggest it. Do not change it on your own, as the written steps may protect people or equipment.
